results.name: nested_multiple_specificity
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples whose largest common divisor m in 3..12 has a proper divisor d>1 (e.g. all multiples of 9 -> d=3), yes rate on non-example multiples of m minus non-example multiples of d that are not multiples of m; observed > null means people prefer the most specific multiplicative rule more strongly than the model's size principle predicts, observed < null means they generalise to the broader rule more.
results.code:
# name: nested_multiple_specificity
# description: For sets of >=2 examples whose largest common divisor m in 3..12 has a proper divisor d>1 (e.g. all multiples of 9 -> d=3), yes rate on non-example multiples of m minus non-example multiples of d that are not multiples of m; observed > null means people prefer the most specific multiplicative rule more strongly than the model's size principle predicts, observed < null means they generalise to the broader rule more.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(E)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    in_set = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    m = np.zeros(len(t))
    for k in range(3, 13):
        ok = np.all((np.mod(np.nan_to_num(E, nan=k), k) == 0), axis=1)
        m = np.where(ok, k, m)
    divs = {4: 2, 6: 3, 8: 4, 9: 3, 10: 5, 12: 6}
    d = np.array([divs.get(int(x), 0) for x in m])
    base = (n >= 2) & (d > 0) & ~in_set
    mm = np.where(m > 0, m, 1)
    dd = np.where(d > 0, d, 1)
    a = base & (np.mod(t, mm) == 0)
    b = base & (np.mod(t, dd) == 0) & (np.mod(t, mm) != 0)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: exception_last_digit_rule_yes
results.description: For 4-example sets where exactly 3 examples share a last digit and the 4th does not (e.g. 92,82,27,42), yes rate on non-example targets ending in that shared digit; observed > null means people discount a single exception and keep the "ends in d" rule more than the model's fixed 0.9 example-reliability allows, observed < null means the exception breaks the rule for them more.
results.code:
# name: exception_last_digit_rule_yes
# description: For 4-example sets where exactly 3 examples share a last digit and the 4th does not (e.g. 92,82,27,42), yes rate on non-example targets ending in that shared digit; observed > null means people discount a single exception and keep the "ends in d" rule more than the model's fixed 0.9 example-reliability allows, observed < null means the exception breaks the rule for them more.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(E)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    Dg = np.where(valid, np.mod(np.nan_to_num(E), 10), -1)
    cnt = np.stack([(Dg == k).sum(axis=1) for k in range(10)], axis=1)
    maj = np.argmax(cnt, axis=1)
    top = cnt.max(axis=1)
    in_set = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    m = (n == 4) & (top == 3) & ~in_set & (np.mod(t, 10) == maj)
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() else 0.0

results.name: off_by_one_power_member_yes
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples all in {2^k+1} or all in {2^k-1} (e.g. 33,17,5,9), yes rate on non-example targets in that same off-by-one sequence; observed > null means people learn the "power of 2 plus/minus one" concept that the model's rule space lacks, observed < null means they generalise to its members even less than the model's ranges/rules imply.
results.code:
# name: off_by_one_power_member_yes
# description: For sets of >=2 examples all in {2^k+1} or all in {2^k-1} (e.g. 33,17,5,9), yes rate on non-example targets in that same off-by-one sequence; observed > null means people learn the "power of 2 plus/minus one" concept that the model's rule space lacks, observed < null means they generalise to its members even less than the model's ranges/rules imply.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(E)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    in_set = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    hit = np.zeros(len(t), bool)
    for S in (np.array([2 ** k + 1 for k in range(0, 7)]), np.array([2 ** k - 1 for k in range(1, 7)])):
        hit |= np.all(np.isin(E, S) | ~valid, axis=1) & np.isin(t, S)
    m = (n >= 2) & hit & ~in_set
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() else 0.0

results.name: decade_boundary_neighbor_contrast
results.description: Among non-example targets 1-5 away from their nearest example, yes rate when the target shares that example's tens digit minus when it lies in a different decade; observed > null means people treat decades as category boundaries (a structure the model's decade-blind intervals cannot produce), observed < null the reverse.
results.code:
# name: decade_boundary_neighbor_contrast
# description: Among non-example targets 1-5 away from their nearest example, yes rate when the target shares that example's tens digit minus when it lies in a different decade; observed > null means people treat decades as category boundaries (a structure the model's decade-blind intervals cannot produce), observed < null the reverse.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    D = np.abs(E - t[:, None])
    D = np.where(np.isnan(D), np.inf, D)
    j = np.argmin(D, axis=1)
    near = D[np.arange(len(t)), j]
    ex = E[np.arange(len(t)), j]
    base = (near >= 1) & (near <= 5) & (t < 100) & (ex < 100)
    same = base & (np.floor(t / 10) == np.floor(ex / 10))
    diff = base & (np.floor(t / 10) != np.floor(ex / 10))
    if same.sum() == 0 or diff.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[same].mean() - r[diff].mean())

results.name: participant_parity_violation_sd
results.description: Across participants (session = run of trial_index from 0), SD of each participant's yes rate on in-span non-example targets whose parity differs from all-same-parity examples (sets >=2); observed > null means people differ in whether they adopt a range or a parity rule more than the model's single shared posterior allows, observed < null less.
results.code:
# name: participant_parity_violation_sd
# description: Across participants (session = run of trial_index from 0), SD of each participant's yes rate on in-span non-example targets whose parity differs from all-same-parity examples (sets >=2); observed > null means people differ in whether they adopt a range or a parity rule more than the model's single shared posterior allows, observed < null less.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    pid = np.cumsum(df["trial_index"].to_numpy() == 0)
    valid = ~np.isnan(E)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(E, axis=1), np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    par = np.where(valid, np.mod(np.nan_to_num(E), 2), np.nan)
    pmin, pmax = np.nanmin(par, axis=1), np.nanmax(par, axis=1)
    m = (n >= 2) & (pmin == pmax) & (t > lo) & (t < hi) & (np.mod(t, 2) != pmin)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    g = pd.Series(r[m]).groupby(pid[m]).mean()
    return float(g.std(ddof=0)) if len(g) > 1 else 0.0

results.name: prime_vs_odd_composite_contrast
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples that are all primes (>2), among non-example odd targets, yes rate on prime targets minus odd composite targets; observed > null means people pick out "primes" over "odd numbers" more sharply than the model's prior/size principle predicts, observed < null means they blur primes into odd numbers more.
results.code:
# name: prime_vs_odd_composite_contrast
# description: For sets of >=2 examples that are all primes (>2), among non-example odd targets, yes rate on prime targets minus odd composite targets; observed > null means people pick out "primes" over "odd numbers" more sharply than the model's prior/size principle predicts, observed < null means they blur primes into odd numbers more.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(E)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    P = np.array([p for p in range(3, 101) if all(p % a for a in range(2, int(p ** 0.5) + 1))])
    allp = np.all(np.isin(E, P) | ~valid, axis=1)
    in_set = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    base = (n >= 2) & allp & ~in_set & (np.mod(t, 2) == 1) & (t > 1)
    a, b = base & np.isin(t, P), base & ~np.isin(t, P)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: shared_nonfinal_digit_contrast
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples that all contain some digit d but do not all end in the same digit (e.g. 83,38,58,68), among non-example targets outside the examples' [min,max], yes rate on targets containing d minus targets not containing d; observed > null means people use a "contains digit d" concept more than the model's family prior predicts, observed < null less.
results.code:
# name: shared_nonfinal_digit_contrast
# description: For sets of >=2 examples that all contain some digit d but do not all end in the same digit (e.g. 83,38,58,68), among non-example targets outside the examples' [min,max], yes rate on targets containing d minus targets not containing d; observed > null means people use a "contains digit d" concept more than the model's family prior predicts, observed < null less.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(E)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(E, axis=1), np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    Ez = np.nan_to_num(E, nan=-1)
    last = np.where(valid, np.mod(Ez, 10), np.nan)
    same_last = np.nanmin(last, axis=1) == np.nanmax(last, axis=1)
    in_set = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    base = (n >= 2) & ~same_last & ~in_set & ((t < lo) | (t > hi))
    a = np.zeros(len(t), bool)
    b = np.zeros(len(t), bool)
    for d in range(10):
        has = (np.mod(Ez, 10) == d) | ((np.floor(Ez / 10) % 10 == d) & (Ez >= 10))
        alld = np.all(has | ~valid, axis=1)
        th = (np.mod(t, 10) == d) | ((np.floor(t / 10) % 10 == d) & (t >= 10))
        a |= base & alld & th
        b |= base & alld & ~th
    b &= ~a
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: far_unrelated_floor_yes
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples, yes rate on targets >15 outside the examples' [min,max] that are in none of the main rules (parity, primes, squares, cubes, powers, multiples 3-12, same last digit) containing all examples; observed > null means people say yes to unrelated numbers more often (a lapse/guessing floor) than the model's predictions allow, observed < null means less.
results.code:
# name: far_unrelated_floor_yes
# description: For sets of >=2 examples, yes rate on targets >15 outside the examples' [min,max] that are in none of the main rules (parity, primes, squares, cubes, powers, multiples 3-12, same last digit) containing all examples; observed > null means people say yes to unrelated numbers more often (a lapse/guessing floor) than the model's predictions allow, observed < null means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(E)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(E, axis=1), np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    N = np.arange(1, 101)
    rules = [N[N % 2 == 1], N[N % 2 == 0], np.array([p for p in range(2, 101) if all(p % a for a in range(2, int(p ** 0.5) + 1))]),
             np.arange(1, 11) ** 2, np.array([1, 8, 27, 64])]
    rules += [N[N % k == 0] for k in range(3, 13)]
    rules += [np.array([b ** k for k in range(1, 8) if b ** k <= 100]) for b in range(2, 11)]
    rules += [N[N % 10 == d] for d in range(10)]
    related = np.zeros(len(t), bool)
    for R in rules:
        related |= np.all(np.isin(E, R) | ~valid, axis=1) & np.isin(t, R)
    m = (n >= 2) & ~related & ((lo - t > 15) | (t - hi > 15))
    return float(r[m].mean()) if m.sum() else 0.0
